name: Utah

sales.rateNote: State sales and use tax of 4.85% (the rate chart splits it into the general state tax and a Medicaid expansion component). Every location adds a 1% local option tax and a 0.25% county option tax, plus other local taxes depending on the area.

local.levies: counties, cities and towns (local option 1%, county option 0.25%, resort community, rural health care, public transit, highways, recreation/zoo/arts and other special taxes)
local.capNote: No single overall cap; each local tax has its own legal rate (e.g. resort communities up to 1.60%, rural health care up to 1%, public transit up to 0.30%).

groceries.note: Grocery food is taxed at a 1.75% state rate; with the 1% local option and 0.25% county option taxes, the combined grocery rate is 3% everywhere in Utah. Other local taxes do not apply to grocery food.

otherRates.note: Reduced state rate on home heating fuels, giving a combined rate of 2.85% less than the general rate.

County tax on restaurant food, imposed by all counties, on top of sales tax; since January 1, 2026 it also covers food prepared or heated to order at grocery stores, convenience stores and gas stations (SB 91, 2025).

sales.holidayNote: Utah does not hold a sales tax holiday; none appears in the Tax Commission's 2025-2026 tax bulletins.

useTax.note: Use tax has the same rates and exemptions as sales tax (state plus local); either sales or use tax applies to a transaction, never both.

facts.text: Groceries are taxed at a flat 3% combined rate everywhere in Utah, whatever the local rate on other goods.
Since January 1, 2026, food prepared or heated at a customer's request in grocery stores, convenience stores and gas stations pays the county restaurant tax (SB 91, 2025).
Resort communities can add up to 1.60%, but sales of vehicles, boats, aircraft and manufactured homes are exempt from that resort tax.
Local rate changes take effect at the start of a calendar quarter: on October 1, 2026, Washington City and Hildale imposed an emergency services tax.
Sales tax returns are due on the last day of the month after the period; businesses with $50,000 or less of annual tax file quarterly.

property.levied: local (counties, cities, school districts and special districts); the county assessor values property and the county treasurer collects

assessment.text: Property is valued at market value as of January 1 each year. A primary residence (including rentals used as full-time homes, with up to one acre of land) receives a 45% exemption, so it is taxed on 55% of market value; vacation homes and cabins are taxed on 100%.

homestead.name: Primary Residential Exemption
homestead.text: 45% of the market value of a qualifying primary residence is exempt (Utah Code 59-2-103). The home must be occupied as a primary domicile for at least 183 consecutive days a year by the owner or a full-time tenant; only one exemption per household.
homestead.applyBy: Handled by the county assessor; a declaration may be required.

otherRelief.name: Homeowner low-income abatement / Homeowner's Credit
otherRelief.text: For owners with 2025 household income under $44,221 who are 67+ or surviving spouses (or qualified in 2025): up to $1,412 abated based on income, plus a credit equal to the tax on 20% of the home's value. Apply to the county by September 1.

otherRelief.name: Veterans with a Disability Exemption
otherRelief.text: Veterans with at least 10% service-connected disability: exemption of up to $535,459 of taxable value, in proportion to the disability rating.

otherRelief.name: Other programs
otherRelief.text: Renter refund, active or reserve duty armed forces exemption, blind exemption, and low-income or elderly deferral.

dueDates.text: Property taxes become delinquent if not paid by November 30; the penalty is 2.5% or $10 per parcel (reduced to 1% or $10 if paid by January 31).

facts.text: Rental homes and apartments used as full-time residences also get the 45% primary residential exemption; second homes and cabins do not.
Home furnishings and furniture are not subject to property tax.
Only one primary residential exemption is allowed per household anywhere in the state.
The state and federal government receive none of Utah's property tax revenue; it funds schools, counties, cities and districts.
Utah offers six types of property tax relief to individuals, administered through county governments.
